body.heading: Tiny muscles at work
paragraphs: Each hair on your skin sits in a small pocket called a follicle, and attached to many follicles is a tiny muscle, the arrector pili. When that muscle contracts, it pulls the hair upright and dimples the skin around it — that bump is a goosebump.

The signal to contract usually comes from your autonomic nervous system, the same automatic system that speeds up your heart when you are startled. You cannot order goosebumps to appear; they arrive on their own.

body.heading: A leftover from furrier ancestors
paragraphs: In animals covered with fur, raised hair traps a thicker layer of air next to the skin, which helps hold in warmth. A cat or dog with raised fur also looks bigger, which can discourage an attacker.
Humans kept the reflex but lost most of the fur that made it useful. Our goosebumps are a quiet reminder that our bodies still run some very old software written for a much hairier life.

body.heading: Why music can trigger them too
paragraphs: Goosebumps are not only about cold. Strong emotions — fear, awe, or a moving piece of music — can set them off, because the same automatic system responds to excitement and surprise, not just temperature.
Researchers sometimes call the pleasant version 'frisson,' the shiver some people feel at a powerful moment in a song. Not everyone experiences it, and that difference is normal.

takeaway: Goosebumps happen when tiny muscles pull your hairs upright — an ancient warming and warning reflex that strong feelings can still trigger.
